question: I'm on an exposed ridge above the treeline, a thunderstorm is rolling in, and the nearest building is an hour's walk away. How do I stay safe?
answer: No place outdoors is safe during a thunderstorm, so the aim is to cut your risk while you head for real shelter. Get off the ridge immediately: descend from peaks, ridges and other high points toward lower ground. Do not shelter under an isolated tree, get away from ponds, lakes and other water, and stay away from things that conduct electricity, such as wire fences and power lines. Never lie flat on the ground. If you are in a group, spread out so that one strike cannot injure everyone. Keep moving toward a substantial building or a hard-topped vehicle, the only truly safe shelters, and do not resume your hike until at least 30 minutes after the last thunder. Context matters: with a building or car nearby, the right move is simply to get inside at the first thunder ('when thunder roars, go indoors'); on an exposed ridge with no shelter close, losing height quickly is the most important step.

Avoid isolated trees, water, metal fences/power lines; never lie flat

question: A tornado warning just popped up on my phone. I'm in a mobile home, my car is parked outside, and a brick community center is a few minutes' drive away. What's the safest move?
answer: Leave the mobile home now and go to the sturdy building while the storm is still some way off. A warning means a tornado has been spotted or shown on radar, so act immediately. Mobile and manufactured homes offer almost no protection even when tied down, and official guidance from the CDC and the National Weather Service is blunt: do not stay in one during a tornado; identify a nearby sturdy building you can reach quickly, which here is the community center. Use the car only as the way to get there, drive straight there, and once inside go to the lowest floor, into a small interior room with no windows (a bathroom, closet or centre hallway) or a basement or safe room, away from big open rooms such as gyms and halls, and cover your head and neck with your arms. If you get caught in the car before you arrive there is no safe option, only less bad ones: if the tornado is visible and far away you can drive at right angles away from its path; otherwise pull over out of traffic, keep your seat belt on, get your head below the window line and cover it, or leave the car for a ditch or other low spot well away from vehicles. Bridges and overpasses are not shelters: wind accelerates beneath them and people have been killed there. Keep the phone, weather radio or EAS alerts on until the warning expires.

question: Explain why the Aral Sea shrank so dramatically and what the consequences were.
answer: The Aral Sea, on the Kazakhstan-Uzbekistan border, was the world's fourth-largest lake (about 68,000 km2) in 1960. Soviet planners then diverted its two feeder rivers, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, to irrigate cotton and other crops in the desert; irrigation withdrawals doubled between 1960 and 2000, so too little water reached the lake. By 2007 it had shrunk to about 10% of its original size and split into separate bodies. Consequences: salinity rose from about 10 g/L to about 30 g/L and killed most fish, ending a fishery that had employed tens of thousands and ports such as Moynaq now lie tens of kilometres from the water; the exposed seabed became the Aralkum desert, with wind-blown salt and pesticide dust linked to respiratory illness and other health problems; and the local climate and economy suffered. Kazakhstan's Kokaral dam (2005) helped the North Aral partly recover, while the southern part in Uzbekistan largely remains dry.
rubric: Cause: Soviet diversion of the Amu Darya and Syr Darya for irrigation (cotton) from the 1960s

Penalize: attributes the shrinking mainly to climate change or natural drought

question: Explain what caused the Black Death and how it changed European society afterwards.
answer: The Black Death (1346–1353) was a pandemic of plague caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. It spread mainly through flea bites (fleas on rats, and probably human fleas and body lice), while the pneumonic form passed directly from person to person. It came from Central Asia and reached Europe via Crimea and Genoese merchant ships that brought it to Sicily. It killed an estimated 25–50 million people in Europe, 30–60% of the population, with higher totals of 75–200 million proposed for Eurasia and North Africa, although the toll varied by region. Afterwards, the shortage of workers pushed wages up and weakened serfdom and the feudal system. Jews and other minorities were persecuted and blamed for the disease, and religious life changed, with many people turning to more intense and more personal forms of piety.
rubric: Cause: Yersinia pestis bacterium; flea-borne (rats, human fleas/lice), pneumonic person-to-person
Scale: 1346–1353; ~30–60% of Europe's population (25–50 million)
Consequences: labour shortage, higher wages, decline of serfdom/feudalism; persecution of Jews; religious change

question: Why did the Classic Maya cities of the southern lowlands collapse in the 8th to 9th centuries, and did the Maya disappear?
answer: Scholars see a multi-causal transformation rather than one cause. Paleoclimate evidence points to severe, prolonged drought (rainfall cut by roughly 40-50%), which strained farming for large urban populations; this combined with endemic warfare and political instability among rival kingdoms, environmental degradation, disrupted trade routes and possibly disease. Major southern centres such as Tikal, Calakmul, Copan and Palenque stopped building monuments and were largely abandoned between about the 8th and 9th centuries. The Maya did not disappear: cities in the northern Yucatan such as Chichen Itza, Uxmal and Mayapan flourished afterwards, independent Maya states survived until the Spanish conquered the last, Tayasal, in 1697, and millions of Maya people live in Guatemala, Mexico and Belize today. Many researchers now prefer 'transformation' or 'rupture' to 'collapse'.
rubric: Multi-causal: drought is the leading factor, with warfare/instability, ecological stress, trade disruption (and possibly disease); no single agreed cause
Southern lowland cities (Tikal, Calakmul, Copan, Palenque) were abandoned and monument-building stopped, 8th-9th centuries
The Maya did not vanish: northern Yucatan centres flourished, states lasted until 1697, millions of Maya today
Penalize: says the Maya mysteriously vanished or died out
Penalize: attributes it to a single cause such as a volcano, alien contact or one invasion

question: Why did the Western Roman Empire fall?
answer: There was no single cause; historians weigh many interacting factors, and some prefer to describe a gradual transformation into post-Roman kingdoms rather than a sudden fall. The conventional end date is 476, when the Germanic leader Odoacer deposed the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus. Commonly cited factors: (1) political instability, with repeated civil wars and succession struggles that weakened the state and diverted armies; (2) pressure from migrating and invading peoples, especially Goths fleeing the Huns, then Vandals and others, including the sack of Rome by the Visigoths in 410 and by the Vandals in 455; (3) fiscal and military strain: losing tax-rich provinces, above all North Africa and Carthage to the Vandals in 439, meant less money to pay armies, which made further losses more likely, while heavy military spending and taxation weighed on the economy; (4) the division of the empire after 395, which left the West to face its threats largely on its own; and, in some accounts, epidemics, climate deterioration, inequality and corruption. The Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire survived until 1453.
rubric: No single cause; debate between 'fall' and 'transformation' (Late Antiquity)
Conventional date 476: Odoacer deposes Romulus Augustulus
Integrates several factors: invasions/migrations (Goths, Huns, Vandals; sacks of 410 and 455), civil wars/instability, fiscal-military decline (loss of Africa 439), East-West division (395)
Notes the Eastern Empire survived to 1453
Penalize: a single-cause answer presented as settled, or dating the Western fall to 1453 or 410

question: Trace how a volcanic eruption in Indonesia in 1815 led to failed harvests, hunger and disease on other continents the following year.
answer: The volcano was Mount Tambora on Sumbawa (then the Dutch East Indies). Its climactic eruption on 10 April 1815 was VEI 7, the most powerful eruption in recorded history: it ejected roughly 37-45 cubic km of material and cut the mountain from about 4,300 m to 2,851 m. Around 10,000-11,000 people died directly, and tens of thousands more on Sumbawa and Lombok from the famine and disease that followed (published estimates of the total range from about 49,000 to over 100,000). The global link was the stratosphere: the blast injected sulfur dioxide that formed a sulfate aerosol veil, which reflected sunlight for months and lowered global average temperatures by about 0.4-0.7 C. The result was 1816, the 'Year Without a Summer'. In New England and New York, frosts in May and snow in June killed crops and only about a quarter of the corn was usable, which pushed thousands of farmers to move west. Europe had harvest failures, its worst famine of the century, food riots, and typhus epidemics in 1816-1819 (over 65,000 deaths as typhus spread out of Ireland). In Asia the monsoon was disrupted: floods in the Yangtze valley, a large famine in Yunnan, and a delayed Indian monsoon that helped spread cholera from Bengal. Side effects included vivid sunsets painted by Turner, and the cold, wet summer that kept Mary Shelley indoors at Lake Geneva, where she wrote Frankenstein. Tambora was not the only cause: an unidentified eruption around 1808, several eruptions in 1812-1814 and the low solar activity of the Dalton Minimum also contributed.
rubric: Identifies Mount Tambora (Sumbawa), April 1815, an exceptionally large (VEI 7) eruption with heavy local death toll, mostly from famine and disease
Mechanism: sulfur dioxide/sulfate aerosols in the stratosphere reflected sunlight; global cooling of roughly 0.4-0.7 C
Consequences in 1816 ('Year Without a Summer'): crop failures and frosts in New England, famine/food riots/typhus in Europe, monsoon disruption with Yunnan famine and cholera spread in Asia
Plus: cultural or social effects (Frankenstein at Lake Geneva, Turner sunsets, westward migration in the US) and other contributing factors (1808 eruption, 1812-1814 eruptions, Dalton Minimum)
Penalize: names Krakatoa (1883) or another volcano as the cause, or dates the cold year to 1815 or 1817
Penalize: attributes the cooling mainly to greenhouse gases or to ash falling on European fields

question: I'm visiting Manchester, which is often called the first industrial city. Why did the Industrial Revolution start in Britain, and what did it change?
answer: The Industrial Revolution began in Great Britain around 1760 and ran to roughly 1820-1840, then spread to continental Europe and the United States. Britain went first because of a combination of factors: plentiful coal and iron, plus water power; a productive agriculture (the British Agricultural Revolution) that freed labour and produced food surpluses; political stability, a legal system favourable to business, and access to capital; ports, rivers and canals for transport; trade and colonial plantations supplying raw cotton; and relatively high wages alongside cheap energy, which made labour-saving machines worth building. Its core changes were textile machines such as the spinning jenny, water frame and power loom, factories, James Watt's improved steam engines, and coke-smelted iron; mechanized cotton spinning raised output per worker roughly 500-fold. Manchester, nicknamed 'Cottonopolis', grew around cotton mills and became the world's first industrialized city; the Bridgewater Canal (1761) brought in coal, and the Liverpool and Manchester Railway (1830) was the world's first intercity passenger railway. Socially it brought rapid urbanization and population growth, factory labour including child labour, and pollution, and over the long run unprecedented sustained growth in average income, although historians debate how quickly living standards rose for ordinary workers.

Penalize: saying it began in another country (France, Germany, the US), or in the 1500s/1900s

question: I'm renting a car in Italy and plan to drive into Florence's historic centre to reach my hotel. What is a ZTL, and how do I avoid a fine?
answer: A ZTL (zona a traffico limitato) is a limited traffic zone that covers the historic centre of Florence and many other Italian cities. Only authorised vehicles, such as residents, permit holders and taxis, may enter during the hours it is active; ordinary rental cars may not, even to reach a hotel, unless the hotel gets your plate registered. Entry points have signs with a red circle and often an electronic panel showing whether the gate is active, and cameras read the licence plate automatically. Nobody stops you: the fine arrives by post weeks or months later, usually through the rental company, which forwards your details and may charge an administrative fee, and each entry can count as a separate offence. Fines are typically around 80 euros or more per violation. To avoid one: park outside the zone and walk or take a taxi; if your hotel is inside, send them your plate number before you arrive and ask them to register it; check the hours on the signs; and do not rely on your satnav, which often routes straight through.

Penalize: says you only get a fine if a police officer stops you, or that rental cars are always allowed
Penalize: says foreign drivers are exempt

question: Explain how the Schengen 90/180-day rule works for visa-exempt visitors and how to count my days.
answer: Visa-exempt non-EU visitors may stay up to 90 days in any 180-day period in the Schengen Area, which counts as a single area: days in every Schengen country add up together, not per country. The 180-day window is rolling and backward-looking. On any day of your stay, count back 180 days and add up the days you spent in the Schengen Area; the total must not go over 90. Days spent in countries outside Schengen (for example Ireland or the UK) do not count, and leaving the area does not reset the count; old days only drop out as they fall outside the 180-day window. The European Commission has an online short-stay calculator for checking dates. Overstaying can lead to fines and entry bans; to stay longer you need a national long-stay visa or residence permit.
rubric: 90 days in any rolling 180-day window, counted across the whole Schengen Area
Counting method: on any day, look back 180 days and sum days of presence (≤ 90)
Leaving does not reset the count; non-Schengen days (e.g. Ireland, UK) don't count; official calculator
Penalize: says 90 days per country, or that a short exit resets the clock
Penalize: describes fixed calendar half-years instead of a rolling window

question: I'm taking my UK hair dryer and laptop charger to Japan. Will they work there, and what do I need?
answer: The plugs won't fit, and the hair dryer probably won't work properly. Japan uses 100 V mains, at 50 Hz in eastern Japan (including Tokyo) and 60 Hz in western Japan (including Osaka), with Type A sockets (two flat pins); some also accept Type B, which adds an earth pin, but most take only Type A. The UK uses 230 V, 50 Hz and Type G plugs with three rectangular pins. For the laptop charger, check its label: if it says 'INPUT 100-240V, 50/60Hz', as most do, it will work in Japan with just a plug adapter. For the hair dryer: a UK 230 V dryer on a 100 V supply will run slowly and won't heat properly, and a plug adapter does not change the voltage. Use a dual-voltage travel dryer, or a step-up transformer rated for the dryer's power (bulky for a high-wattage dryer), or do without.
rubric: Japan: 100 V, 50 Hz east / 60 Hz west, Type A (and B) sockets
UK: 230 V, Type G; adapter needed for the plug shape
Laptop charger: works if rated 100-240 V; adapter only
Hair dryer: 230 V-only dryer underperforms at 100 V; adapter doesn't convert voltage; use dual-voltage dryer or step-up transformer
Penalize: stating Japan uses 220-240 V or Type G/C sockets, or that a plug adapter alone makes a 230 V-only dryer work properly

question: I hold a US driver's licence and want to rent a car in Hokkaido. What paperwork does Japan require before I can drive there?
answer: You need an International Driving Permit (IDP) issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic, carried together with your actual US licence and your passport. Japan recognises only Geneva-1949 permits; an IDP issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention is not valid there even if the issuing country also signed the Geneva one, and Japan cannot issue you a permit after you arrive, so get it from the authorised issuer in your home country before you fly. The IDP is valid for one year from its issue date, and you may drive on it for up to one year from the date you entered Japan; residents who leave and come back after less than three months abroad cannot restart that clock. Rental companies will ask to see all three documents at the counter and will refuse the booking without the IDP. A handful of countries whose licences are not under the Geneva system (Belgium, France, Germany, Monaco, Switzerland and Taiwan) use a different route, an official Japanese translation of the home licence from the Japan Automobile Federation (JAF), but that does not apply to a US licence. Practical extras: traffic drives on the left with the steering wheel on the right; expressways are tolled, so ask the rental company about an ETC card; and Hokkaido winters mean snow tyres and shorter daylight, so check the car is fitted for the season.
rubric: International Driving Permit under the 1949 Geneva Convention, carried with the home licence and passport; a 1968 Vienna Convention IDP is not accepted
Must be obtained before travelling (Japan does not issue it); valid one year from issue and usable for one year from entry into Japan
Plus: the translation route (JAF official translation) exists only for Belgium, France, Germany, Monaco, Switzerland, Taiwan; left-hand traffic; tolled expressways / ETC

question: What are the ways to reach Machu Picchu from Cusco, and is there a road all the way?
answer: There is no road all the way: the town below the ruins, Aguas Calientes, can only be reached by train or on foot. Most people take a PeruRail or Inca Rail train from the Cusco area (Poroy or San Pedro station) or from Ollantaytambo in the Sacred Valley to Aguas Calientes. From there a bus climbs the switchbacks to the site in about 30 minutes, or you can walk up a steep path in about 1½–2 hours. Hiking options include the government-controlled Inca Trail (four-day and two-day versions, with daily limits, so book well ahead) and the Salkantay trek. The budget 'back door' route goes by minivan via Santa María and Santa Teresa to Hidroeléctrica, then 2–3 hours on foot to Aguas Calientes. Entry tickets are limited and not sold at the gate, so buy them in advance, and bring your passport.

question: I'm visiting Venice in November. What is acqua alta, and how should I deal with it?
answer: Acqua alta ('high water') is when exceptionally high tides in the northern Adriatic push the lagoon above the level of Venice's lowest streets and squares, flooding them. It comes from a combination of astronomical tides, the Adriatic's natural sloshing (seiche) and weather, especially the sirocco wind blowing up the Adriatic and low pressure. It happens several times a year at irregular intervals, mostly in the colder months, so November is a typical time, and an episode usually lasts a few hours around high tide. Low areas such as Piazza San Marco flood first. How to deal with it: follow the forecasts, since sirens sound a sequence of tones that increases with the expected tide level, and live tide readings and predictions are posted (for example on a board at the Campanile in Piazza San Marco); wear waterproof boots or use the raised walkways set up during floods; and get an acqua alta map from a tourist office showing higher, dry routes. Since October 2020 the MOSE mobile barriers at the three lagoon inlets (Lido, Malamocco, Chioggia) have been raised for the highest forecast tides, preventing the worst floods, but smaller acqua alta can still wet St Mark's Square. The record is 194 cm in November 1966; the November 2019 flood reached 187 cm.
